title: Why CS programs shouldn't teach Git, and how ThePrimeagen uses rebase, git internals, and a trade-school model
summary: ThePrimeagen explains why he wrote a Git course starting at internals, argues schools should teach how version control works rather than just using it, and defends rebasing your own branches (with rerere). He also sketches a trade-school alternative to bootcamps and CS degrees, and shares fast-and-sloppy build habits.

principles.text: Learn Git internals first; once you know every commit holds the whole tree, the rest of Git makes sense.
principles.quote: it get as every single commit contains the entire tree all of a sudden things start making more sense you can kind of guess how these things work

principles.text: Small tool knowledge saves real pain: learn the cheap undo commands instead of abort-and-redo for years.
principles.quote: it's just like these little things that you learn that are just like so useful with just knowing get that will just save you these little teeny tiny pieces of pain

principles.text: Schools should teach how version control is built, not just how to use Git, like every other CS foundation course.
principles.quote: data structures they don't teach you about using data structures they teach you how to implement it and then explain why it's this way

principles.text: Rebase and squash feature work into one commit so a bad change can be reverted cleanly; always bet against yourself.
principles.quote: I always program with the one uh fundamental uh philosophy which is always bet against yourself and so when I program I believe I'm going to screw it up

principles.text: Rewriting history is fine on your own branches; never change the history of the shared main line.
principles.quote: in my branches like I own reality I just decide what reality I the god of my own branches

principles.text: Work fast and sloppy, since you never get it right the first try, then rebuild with the unknowns removed.
principles.quote: I'd rather work fast and sloppy and clean up later then work perfect and slow and then realize all my perfection was wrong anyways
